titulo: Managing a Conversation: Turn-Taking, Interrupting, Repair
subtitulo: Running the conversation, not just your turns
descripcion: At C2 you manage a conversation's overall shape, not just your own turns: noticing when someone hasn't spoken and drawing them in, redirecting a conversation that's drifted without announcing the redirection, and repairing someone else's stumble without drawing attention to it.

filas: So, coming back to the original question…
picking up their unfinished sentence naturally

ejemplos.texto: What's your read on this? You've been quiet.
So, coming back to the original question, where does that leave us?
—I think what you mean is that it needs more time.

notas: Drawing in someone who hasn't spoken is a management move, not just politeness — it changes what the conversation as a whole produces.
Redirecting without announcing it (so, coming back to…) is smoother than explicitly calling out the drift, which can feel like a correction.
Finishing someone else's stumbled sentence accurately and briefly helps them; doing it repeatedly or inaccurately undermines them.

es.en: Spanish has phrases for the same moves («¿tú qué opinas, Ana?» – what's your take, Ana?; «volviendo a lo de antes» – going back to…), so the functions transfer. The work lies in building a ready repertoire of English phrases for each move.
es.es: El español tiene expresiones para las mismas funciones («¿tú qué opinas, Ana?» – «what's your take, Ana?»; «volviendo a lo de antes» – «going back to…»), por lo que la función se transfiere. El trabajo consiste en construir un repertorio listo de expresiones inglesas para cada movimiento.

de.en: German has phrases for the same moves («Was meinen Sie dazu?» – What's your take?; «um noch mal auf… zurückzukommen» – going back to…). One difference: English meetings often use first names even in formal settings, where German would use «Sie» and a surname.
de.de: Deutsch hat Formeln für dieselben Gesprächsschritte («Was meinen Sie dazu?» – «What's your take?»; «um noch mal auf… zurückzukommen» – «going back to…»). Ein Unterschied: In englischen Meetings werden auch in formellen Kontexten häufig Vornamen verwendet, wo Deutsch «Sie» und den Nachnamen benutzen würde.

it.en: Italian has phrases for the same moves («tu che ne pensi?» – what's your take?; «tornando a…» – going back to…), so the functions transfer directly.
it.it: L'italiano ha espressioni per le stesse funzioni («tu che ne pensi?» – «what's your take?»; «tornando a…» – «going back to…»), quindi le funzioni si trasferiscono direttamente.

fr.en: French has phrases for the same moves («et toi, qu'en penses-tu ?» – what's your take?; «pour revenir à…» – going back to…), so the functions transfer directly.
fr.fr: Le français possède des expressions pour les mêmes mouvements («et toi, qu'en penses-tu ?» – «what's your take?» ; «pour revenir à…» – «going back to…»), donc les fonctions se transfèrent directement.

pt.en: Portuguese has phrases for the same moves («e tu, o que achas?» – what's your take?; «voltando a…» – going back to…), so the functions transfer directly.
pt.pt: O português tem expressões para os mesmos movimentos («e você, o que acha?» – «what's your take?»; «voltando a…» – «going back to…»), então as funções se transferem diretamente.

errores: Redirecting so abruptly that it reads as a correction rather than a smooth return.
Finishing someone else's sentences so often that it takes over the conversation.
Drawing in a quiet person in a way that puts them on the spot rather than genuinely inviting them.

es: «*A ver*» as a turn-taking opener rendered as *To see…* instead of *Let's see…* or *Right…*.
de: «*Moment mal*» rendered as *Moment once* instead of *Hang on a second*.
it: «*Allora*» as a turn-taking opener rendered as *Then…* instead of *So…* or *Right…*.
fr: «*Attends*» rendered as a bare *Wait*, which sounds abrupt, instead of *Hang on a second*.
pt: «*Espera aí*» rendered as *Wait there* instead of *Hang on a second*.

mision.consigna: Describe how you would steer a dinner conversation about money where one person dominates and another says nothing.
requisitos: drawing in a silent participant without spotlighting them
one redirection that is never announced as such
one repair of a misunderstanding between two others
use *disposable income*, *to be frugal* and *to live hand to mouth*

microtareas.texto: Write three ways to bring someone in without *You haven't said anything*.
Write a redirect that sounds like a continuation, not a correction.
Record 2 minutes on *a windfall*: what would you do with it? Invite the listener in twice.

autochequeo: Has a quiet participant been drawn in naturally, not put on the spot?
Is any redirection smooth rather than an explicit correction?
Is a completed sentence for someone else accurate and brief?
Does the conversation as a whole feel managed, not just my own turns?
Have I avoided taking over by finishing sentences too often?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on managing the conversation as a whole: drawing others in, redirecting smoothly, repairing others' stumbles. Do not rewrite the text. Flag anything that feels abrupt or unnatural.
